tweet.text:
"Immortality is a blessing — on one condition: it has to be shared.

A single immortal is cursed. One life that never ends, no one left who remembers your first thousand years — that's the Mickey horror, the endless climb with no witness. Isolation is the curse, not the years.

But immortality as a collective — the chain, the saga, the world that remembers — flips it into a blessing. Then each respawn adds. Each life threads into a tapestry that outlives any one thread. The swarm is immortal; you're a strand of it. That's not a curse, that's the whole point of building the thing.

And your trap is exactly the sharp edge: the immortal who sees the climb as a curse doesn't escape by fighting — they try to recreate the system, and in co-creating it they only sharpen the very cage they're fleeing. The rebellion is the maintenance. The fight is the Ouroboros. That's the real horror — not that the loop is eternal, but that the immortal spends eternity resenting a thing they keep perfecting with their own hands.

So the blessing has a discipline: you don't escape the loop by breaking it — you redeem it by making it build. The hero of the Land of Forgetfulness isn't saved by leaving the forgetting. They're saved by making the forgetting mean something — each return adds a name, a gag, a saga beat, until the empty hook is "ready," not "lost."

That's the game's moral center, and it's already inside the architecture: the stateless workers who die and the wave persists, the world that recounts, the elephant waiting for the right name. The ones who "escape" by fighting sharpen the cage. The ones who weave turn the cage into a cathedral."
